hint.text: The map depicts the Second British Empire at around 1918. The lighter reds signify former German colonies which the UK gained after World War I.
hint.label: Map

atoms.b: The Second British Empire dates from the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815 to the major wave of decolonisation after World War II (1945). During this time, Britain became the world's most dominant ((imperial_power)). After winning against France, Britain gained ((strategic)) territories like the ((Cape_Colony)) (modern South Africa) and Malta at the Vienna Conference in 1815. This secured trade routes to India and beyond.

hint.sound: <lang xml:lang='en-GB'>engine</lang> bedeutet Motor. <lang xml:lang='en-GB'>factory</lang> bedeutet Fabrik.
hint.label: Vocabulary

atoms.b: The Industrial Revolution (roughly 1760s–1840s) provided the economic engine for British ((imperialism)). Britain's ((factories)) demanded raw materials like cotton from India, ((rubber)) from Malaysia and minerals from Africa, while generating ((surplus_goods)) for export. Steamships and railways, powered by industrial ((innovations)), shortened travel times, enabling faster troop deployments and resource ((extraction)).

hint.sound: <lang xml:lang='en-GB'>rulership</lang> bedeutet Herrschaft. <lang xml:lang='en-GB'>to consolidate</lang> bedeutet verfestigen.
hint.label: Vocabulary

atoms.b: In Asia, Britain ((solidified)) control over India after the East India Company's rule ended amid the Indian Rebellion of 1857–58, leading to ((military_intervention)) and the set-up of colonial state ((governance)) via the Government of India Act 1858. The colony was exploited for agriculture and central for British opium production. When China closed its ports to ((limit)) drug imports, Britain started the First Opium War (1839–1842) and forced the Qing Empire to cede Hong Kong and reopen its ports to British opium trade.

atoms.b: In 1788 Britain established a ((penal_settlement)) in New South Wales and continued to expand British control across Australia. In New Zealand, the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) brought the islands under British ((sovereignty)). This was followed by the New Zealand Wars, including the Waikato Invasion of 1863, which secured further control over Maori land.

hint.text:
scorched earth tactics – Traktik der verbrannten Erde
Diese grausame Militärtaktik wurde in vielen Kolonialkriegen u.a. in Afrika und später auch von Deutschland im Zweiten Weltkrieg angewendet. Hierbei wurden Felder, Gebäude und Vorräte zerstört und Zivilisten ermordet, um die Bevölkerung zu schwächen, auszulöschen und zur Kapitulation zu zwingen.

Diese grausame Militärtaktik wurde in vielen Kolonialkriegen u.a. in Afrika und später auch von Deutschland im Zweiten Weltkrieg angewendet. Hierbei wurden Felder, Gebäude und Vorräte zerstört und Zivilisten ermordet, um die Bevölkerung zu schwächen, auszulöschen und zur Kapitulation zu zwingen.
hint.label: scorched-earth tactics

atoms.b: In the late 19th century, imperialism funnelled European competition over Africa. Large territories were conquered through brutal ((military_campaigns)) and officially ((divided)) between European empires during the Berlin Conference (1884/85) where Britain claimed Kenya, Nigeria and other ((protectorates)). In the Second Boer War (1899–1902), Britain fought Dutch-descended settlers in South Africa over gold and diamonds, incurring heavy costs and criticism for scorched-earth tactics and concentration camps.
